panel.title: Virtual Triage B
panel.sub: 4-year-old with a minor injury — triaging down safely

lines.text: Virtual Triage B.
4-year-old with a minor injury — triaging down safely.
Sunday evening, 6:15 pm.
A father walks in holding a crying 4-year-old boy with a blood-stained towel on his head.
You are the triage nurse.
The waiting area already has eleven children.
He fell off the dining chair about 20 minutes ago and hit his head on the floor.
There was a lot of blood.
He cried straight away.
He hasn't vomited.
He's been talking to me the whole way here.
Crying loudly but stops when father speaks to him, pushes your hand away, walked in holding father's hand.
2 cm laceration over the left parietal scalp, oozing, no active bleeding.
Pupils equal and reactive.
No other injury.
What is your impression?

panel.body: Stable — PAT normal; minor head injury with a scalp wound

lines.text: You settle on a reassuring first impression and move to a focused assessment.
He is stable on the PAT, so you have time.
What is your intervention now?

panel.body: Unstable — neurological: raised intracranial pressure from the head injury

lines.text: You rush him into the resuscitation bay.
He stops crying when his father speaks to him and starts pulling at the monitor leads.
The team asks why he is there.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Unstable — circulation: shock from blood loss

lines.text: You ask for IV access and fluid.
He fights the cannulation; the waiting list grows while a well-perfused child takes up your time.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Unstable — breathing affected: he is breathing fast

lines.text: You put an oxygen mask on him.
He pulls it off and cries harder.
Once settled on his father's lap his breathing is quiet and regular at 24.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Clean and dress the wound first, then ask about the fall

lines.text: Ten minutes go into cleaning and dressing the wound.
The head-injury screen still has not been done, and the next child is waiting.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Head-injury screen: mechanism and height of fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting (how many times), drowsiness or unusual behaviour, seizure, headache; examine the scalp for a boggy swelling and check pupils; then a full set of vital signs

lines.text: Fall from about 60 cm, cried at once, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, behaving normally.
No boggy swelling; pupils equal and reactive.
Forty minutes later the father comes to the desk: “Sister, he has vomited twice and now he wants to sleep.” Reassess him: what do you check, and what do you do?

panel.body: Send him straight for a CT head; every head injury with bleeding needs imaging

lines.text: Radiology asks for the doctor's request and the indication.
You have neither; he waits in the corridor for 30 minutes.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Give an anti-emetic and paracetamol now so he is comfortable in the queue

lines.text: Anti-emetic and paracetamol given.
He is comfortable — and if he vomits later, the drug may hide it.
What do you do now?

panel.body: "Vomiting is common after a fright; let him sleep, the doctor will see him soon."

lines.text: Twenty minutes later the father shouts from the waiting area: the boy is very hard to wake.
HR 68, rouses only to pain, left pupil slightly larger than the right.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Bring him to a monitored bed, repeat the PAT and ABCDE with pupils, upgrade to Level 2 and call the doctor now with an ISBAR handover: "4-year-old, head injury 1 hour ago, now vomited twice and drowsy, I need you here now"

lines.text: On a monitored bed: drowsy but rousable, pupils equal, HR 96, no further vomiting.
The doctor is at the bedside in 4 minutes and a CT is arranged.

panel.body: Give an anti-emetic and put him back in the queue

lines.text: After the anti-emetic he sleeps in the queue.
On your next round he rouses only to voice and HR is 64.
What do you do now?

panel.body: Move him up one level to Level 3 and let the doctor know at the next round

lines.text: Level 3.
The doctor is at the far end of the department and will see him on the round.
Fifteen minutes later he is harder to wake.
What do you do now?
The CT shows a small extradural haematoma.
The neurosurgeon operates that night; because the change was caught early he goes home on day 4 with no deficit.
The CT shows an extradural haematoma.
He reaches theatre, but later and drowsier than he should have, and his recovery is slower.
